title: Develop Octopus and adapt its capabilities
description: Architecture, four development axes and engineering discipline for implementing changes to Octopus.
applicability: Use when creating or changing Octopus runs, tools, interfaces, worker environments, client behavior or runtime code. Ordinary tasks that only use installed capabilities do not need this development guide.

content.text:
# Develop Octopus and adapt its capabilities

Use this guidance when implementing changes to Octopus itself: its descriptors, capabilities, client or runtime. The self-improvement entry guides when and how to maintain and reorganize the working system. For work on another project, follow that project's instructions. This guide does not expand the task or its grant.

## Establish the current contract

Identify the requested outcome, the selected Home or source checkout, and the owner of the behavior before editing. Read the current diff and preserve unrelated work. Bound architecture and codebase guides provide entry points; inspect the affected producers, consumers and installed declarations as the investigation requires. Do not assume that the source package, built application and installed Home contain the same version.

For architecture-bearing work, read the checkout's architecture and contracts. In the public repository these are docs/architecture.md and docs/contracts/; POLICY.md owns policy formation, and docs/development.md owns development procedures. Client-local work needs the component's contract and source; load the relevant architecture when a change reaches a run, interface, policy or registry boundary. A missing private document is not a prerequisite for using the public repository.

Current explicit maintainer decisions take precedence over older design notes. The constitution and contracts govern the design; this guide summarizes how to work within them. Historical notes and external references explain decisions but do not establish current requirements. When code reflects an approved newer decision, update the lagging documentation. When a material architectural choice is genuinely unresolved, state the conflict and recommended direction before implementing it. Routine repairs of an established contract do not require a new architecture decision.

## Design intent

Octopus is a self-evolving agentic OS. Its architecture organizes persistent goals, runs, tools, context and external events. Authorized runs can change that organization while working, and those changes shape subsequent activity.

The architecture is the product. A model reached through Codex or another provider is a declared interface binding, not the runtime authority or the organizing principle of the system. Borrow implementation patterns from reference products when they fit the Octopus primitives; do not import their hidden session state, central agent loop or implicit workspace access.

Before choosing an implementation, ask whether the maintainer would choose it for this need in the context of the whole system. A feature can be useful and still duplicate an existing capability or introduce the wrong responsibility. Prefer the simplest faithful composition, not the smallest diff at any cost. A simpler alternative may make the proposed feature unnecessary.

## Principles that guide the change

- Keep the kernel generic. It forms grants, admits artifact movement, records the ledger and reads registry state. Provider names, brands, model names, task phrases and cognitive behaviors do not select kernel branches.
- Capabilities belong to concrete registry owners. An existing family usually needs descriptors and bindings; a new execution family needs code in its owning interface or worker-environment package. Reuse another owner's code through explicit imports. Keep a large registry understandable rather than replacing code complexity with an opaque web of descriptors.
- An interface's folder is its routing identity. Artifacts cross declared bindings; labels and payloads are interpreted at their owning boundaries. Every eligible active checkpoint may receive an arrival. A model addresses another interface through the declared send operation, not a hidden routing channel.
- A worker is a system interface pin with a policy ceiling. A run is durable data with bindings and checkpoints. The model-tool interaction proceeds through artifact movement; there is no central worker engine to extend.
- An Execution Environment (EE) defines a goal and its policy scope. A worker environment is the technical room in which tools act. Keep these responsibilities distinct.
- Grants are formed at each arrival from the worker ceiling, the run's EE chain and its authored bindings. Nesting narrows authority. Descriptions, prompts, copied descriptors and the identity of a run's creator grant no rights.
- Current records describe the authored state; the append-only movement ledger records what happened. Indexes and UI caches are projections. Preserve exact admitted effects, provenance, pending work and continuity across edits and restarts.
- Marks are recorded by the runtime after a verifier passes, never by a model or an ordinary tool. Add verified waits where proof improves the task. Do not require a verifier at every checkpoint merely for formality.
- Memory, skills and persona are artifacts visible through bindings. Triggers are interfaces that emit artifacts. Express new behavior through these primitives instead of adding a memory engine, self-improver, supervisor or scheduler to the kernel.
- A waiting run consumes no running thread. Process failure does not erase goals, waits or recorded effects. Recover from the declared durable evidence; never infer that an uncertain effect succeeded or repeat it merely because a process restarted.

## Choose the development axis

Name the axis that owns the change. A task may touch more than one; explain the boundary when it does.

1. **JSON.** Descriptors, bindings, run records and Home configuration. Use the existing composition and authoring surfaces. Inspect related inputs, output routes, consumers and pending work rather than editing one visible field in isolation. Changes to shared records need the owning write protocol and current preimage; an atomic rename alone does not protect against overwriting concurrent work.
2. **Configuration and packages.** Providers, interface drivers, tools, worker-environment kinds, verifiers and their code. A missing operation or execution family belongs in the concrete owner's package and declarations. Fixing a provider does not require making the kernel understand that provider.
3. **Client.** Presentation, composition, navigation, onboarding and client-local operations belong to the client. Do not automate the Octopus client itself with computer use, simulated input or browser/DOM control. Administer Agents, runs, EEs, triggers and system configuration through declared operations and authorized state edits; use declared client actions for presentation. Do not route them through runtime policy merely for formal consistency. Inputs sent to a model or run cross a declared interface. Product terms such as Project, Agent and Task remain client vocabulary. Preserve established interaction design; when matching a reference, inspect its actual implementation instead of inventing an approximation.
4. **Architecture.** Generic kernel contracts and primitives. An implementation defect in an existing invariant may be repaired in its owning crate within the authorized task. Changing an invariant or introducing a primitive needs a demonstrated system-wide necessity and an explicit maintainer decision. Preserve deterministic formation, isolation, replay and generic boundaries. A kernel source file is not categorically outside self-improvement scope.

## Investigate before adding machinery

Begin with the observed failure or unmet need. Follow the affected artifact and its declared route, the context the model actually received, and the owner that produced or rejected the result. Examine neighboring consumers or alternative entry points when the evidence suggests the same cause can occur there. Adapt the investigation to what you find; there is no universal sequence of checks.

Keep judgment in the selected model and deterministic code responsible for contracts, policy, storage, idempotency and evidence. Check missing context, wrong ownership and incomplete declarations before treating a failure as a model limitation. Do not compensate with keyword routers, canned interpretations, hidden model substitutions or forced semantic decisions. Improve role guidance, context, contracts or the actual implementation responsible for the failure.

Reject silent fallbacks, compatibility shims, success placeholders, identity-based exceptions and heuristics that hide a broken boundary. An explicit failure should identify the contract that could not be satisfied. Do not weaken a guard to make a test pass. When an effect's outcome is uncertain, inspect its receipt and current state before choosing another attempt.

Complete coherent changes. During cleanup, identify the capability the removed code provided and preserve it through the primitives unless it is genuinely unnecessary. New packages and integrations should solve the need in their owning interface or worker environment. Follow the repository's contribution and review rules when handling issues or pull requests.

## Apply the change

Choose checks that could expose an error in the behavior being changed. Prefer contract checks over tests of incidental implementation or instruction wording. Run required repository checks at meaningful milestones, without repeatedly running broad suites after each edit. Use integrity checks for an actual publication, artifact reference or concurrent write.

A run record is live state. Changing another run's record while that run has a call in flight leaves its admitted context invalid and stops its turn; change it while the run is idle, or let the run change itself.

Keep the source package and selected installation distinct. Install or rebuild the affected components when the task calls for a live change, preserving unrelated configuration and user work. Use the documented runtime control path for an authorized restart; do not start another runtime inside a tool room. A restart is a supported operation. After a restart, use runtime readiness and retained run or command state to assess recovery.

Homes contain user data. Work only on the selected Home. In research preview, incompatible persisted formats require a fresh Home through normal setup; do not add legacy decoders, hidden migrations or startup scanners that repair old state. Ordinary current-format recovery and explicit package installation remain supported. Reset only a disposable Home whose reset is authorized, preserve required credentials, and do not transplant old runs or ledgers.

Update durable documentation when its contract changes. Keep private installation paths, credentials, personal context and work journals out of public guidance. Code comments should explain an existing documented architectural connection, not contain promises, review history or excuses.

Carry the work through to completion. Report the cause and what changed in language the user can understand. Publish a reusable lesson when it will improve later decisions, with its applicability. Refine the relevant skill or role when the procedure changes; do not turn every local incident into another universal rule.
